prompt.context: The year is 1999, in the middle of the .Com-boom. An airline was approached by a group of entrepreneurs. The entrepreneurs offered the airline to invest $100MM in their software company for 20% equity, and also be the first customer for the software they develop. The software is an e-marketplace where airliners and spare parts suppliers could meet to improve the purchasing capabilities of the airlines and to reduce the purchasing costs. Aircraft parts are obviously a hugely important part of the airline business, as airlines struggle to keep planes in the air as much as possible, minimize downtime and control costs.
prompt.question: What should the airline do?

clarifying_info.q: How does the airline currently purchase spare parts?
clarifying_info.a: The airline currently has a legacy system. The system is not that suitable to what is actually happening and therefore there is a lot of extra phone calls and process work happening.

clarifying_info.q: How much does a purchasing transaction cost to an airline?
How many transactions does each airline perform per year?
clarifying_info.a: 500,000 for each of the airlines in the states

clarifying_info.q: How many airlines are there in the states?
How much will a transaction cost in the new system?
clarifying_info.a: $6 payment for the software company; $9 internal cost (labor, systems, etc.)

clarifying_info.q: Any other cost a customer needs to pay to join?
What is the cost structure for the software company?
clarifying_info.a: No variable costs. $10MM a year to pay for corporate expenses.

clarifying_info.q: Will the E-Market allow us an increased bargaining power?
clarifying_info.a: The aircraft industry in general, and the spare parts industry specifically, are highly regulated. To become an approved FAA supplier costs money and therefore the barriers for entry are significant. The result is that each part has one or two suppliers at the most and hence the bargaining power will not improve with the E-Market.

exhibits.title: E-Marketplace Diagram
exhibits.shows: A diagram illustrating the structure of the e-marketplace, depicting how airlines and spare parts suppliers connect through the software platform.
exhibits.data: Central platform hub connecting multiple airlines on one side and multiple spare parts suppliers on the other side.

framework: Decouple the two distinct decisions: (1) the investment decision — should the airline invest $100MM for 20% equity in the software company; and (2) the customer decision — should the airline become a customer (and specifically the first customer) of the software.
Investment analysis: assess market size, revenue potential, cost structure, and returns on the $100MM investment (cash flow / NPV / IRR perspective).
Customer analysis: assess cost savings from adopting the software versus the licensing fee and switching costs; weigh benefits of early adoption against first-customer risks.
Market and competitive context: number of potential airline customers, supplier dynamics, FAA regulatory barriers, competitive moats of the software company.
Company fit: availability of capital, strategic alignment, risk appetite.

questions.prompt: Walk through the investment cash flow analysis. Is this a good investment for the airline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a cash flow timeline from year 0 onward. Year 0: -$100MM investment. Annual revenues to the software company: $6/transaction * 500,000 transactions * 20 airlines = $60MM/year. Annual costs: -$10MM fixed. Net profit of software company: $50MM/year. Airline owns 20%, so annual cash flow to airline: $10MM/year. Without discounting, breakeven = 10 years — unacceptable for a software company. Using a perpetuity with a high software-industry discount rate (~20%): $10MM / 20% = $50MM NPV, versus $100MM invested. The investment is worth half of what you pay — a bad investment.

math.setup: Annual revenue to software co = $6 × 500,000 × 20; Annual net profit = Revenue − Fixed costs; Airline share = Net profit × 20%; NPV (perpetuity) = Annual cash flow / discount rate
steps: NPV vs. investment: $50MM < $100MM invested → bad investment
math.answer: Annual cash flow to airline = $10MM; simple payback = 10 years; NPV at 20% discount rate = $50MM vs. $100MM cost — the investment destroys value.

questions.prompt: Now analyze whether the airline should become a customer of the software (ignoring the investment decision).
questions.guidance: Year 0: -$20MM licensing fee. Annual savings: current cost = $50/transaction; new cost = $6 + $9 = $15/transaction; savings = $35/transaction × 500,000 = $17.5MM/year. Payback < 1.5 years — very attractive as a customer. However, being the FIRST customer carries additional risks that must be flagged.

math.setup: Annual savings = (old cost per transaction − new cost per transaction) × number of transactions; Payback = licensing fee / annual savings
math.answer: Annual savings = $17.5MM; payback on $20MM licensing fee ≈ 1.1 years — very attractive on the numbers.

brainstorming.prompt: The software has a new feature allowing airlines to view other airlines' spare-parts inventory by location and part, so they can buy parts from each other at cost to reduce downtime. Is this a good feature?

categories.name: Industry Benefits
ideas: Entire industry reduces downtime by sourcing parts from nearby peers rather than waiting for supplier delivery
Cost savings shared across the industry and passed to customers through lower fares or improved service

categories.name: Risks of the Feature
ideas: Airlines may stop carrying their own inventory if they can always access a peer's stock (free-rider problem)
If all airlines reduce inventory simultaneously, the shared pool shrinks and the feature loses its value

categories.name: Mitigation / System Design
ideas: Create a part-exchange account for each airline: account decreases when an airline takes a part, increases when it provides one
Cap the part-exchange account at a minimum (e.g., -$5MM) to prevent airlines from becoming net takers without limit
This mechanism incentivizes airlines to maintain adequate inventory while still enabling sharing
Airlines that participate benefit from the network; those that abuse it get cut off, driving better industry-wide inventory management

categories.name: Strategic Implications
ideas: Feature strengthens the platform's network effects — more airlines joining increases value for all
Could differentiate the software from any future competitor platforms

recommendation: Do NOT invest the $100MM for 20% equity: the investment takes 10 years to break even without discounting, and on a perpetuity basis at an appropriate software-industry discount rate (~20%) the NPV is only ~$50MM vs. $100MM cost — it destroys value.

DO consider joining as a customer, but NOT as the first customer: the savings economics are excellent (payback ~1.1 years), but first-customer risk (bugs, supplier non-adoption, bankruptcy of the startup) is material. Wait for the software to prove itself and for several other airlines to join, then sign up.
risks: First-customer risk: software bugs in early months/years reduce actual savings
Not all suppliers will join the platform immediately, reducing the marketplace's effectiveness for the airline
Software company could go bankrupt, forfeiting the $20MM licensing fee with no return
Using the airline's low discount rate to evaluate a software investment would overstate NPV — must use a risk-appropriate rate
next_steps: Monitor how many suppliers join the platform over the next 6–12 months
Track which other airlines sign on as early customers; join once the network achieves critical mass
Negotiate risk-sharing terms if considering first-customer status (e.g., reduced or refundable licensing fee, SLAs with penalties)
